summary: In this episode, the hosts conclude their three-part series on the Fall of Man by examining the Tower of Babel narrative in Genesis 11. They argue that this story is not merely a myth but a biblical retelling of the founding of Babylon, a historical event known to the ancient audience. The hosts explore the etymology of Babel, connecting it to the Akkadian 'Bab-ilu' meaning 'Gate of the Gods,' and show how the biblical author deliberately reinterprets this name to mean 'confusion' (from the Hebrew 'balal'), making a theological commentary on Babylon's imperial ambitions. They discuss the historical founding of Babylon around 2300 BC, its rise as the first world empire under Hammurabi, and its eventual collapse, which they interpret as God's judgment on human pride and idolatry.

entities.title: Babylon
entities.summary: An ancient city in Mesopotamia, founded around 2300 BC, which became the capital of the first world empire under Hammurabi. In the Bible, it symbolizes human pride, idolatry, and opposition to God.

entities.title: Hammurabi
entities.summary: King of Babylon in the 18th century BC, known for his law code. He established Babylon as the capital of the first empire, uniting Mesopotamia and creating a cosmopolitan trade network.

entities.title: Nimrod
entities.summary: A biblical figure described as a mighty hunter and the first ruler of Babylon. The hosts connect him to the giants of Genesis 6 and the Mesopotamian god Ninurta, suggesting he represents the resurgence of the antediluvian giants.

entities.title: Eber
entities.summary: An ancestor of Abraham, from whom the Hebrews derive their name. Mentioned in the genealogies, he is part of the lineage leading to Israel.

entities.title: Marduk
entities.summary: The chief god of Babylon, associated with the planet Jupiter. He was worshipped as the son of the sun god Shamash, and his cult was central to Babylonian religion.

entities.title: Shamash
entities.summary: The sun god in Semitic mythology, worshipped in Babylon. He was considered the most high god, but was later overshadowed by Marduk.

concepts.title: Tower of Babel
concepts.summary: The Tower of Babel is a biblical narrative in Genesis 11:1-9 explaining the origin of diverse languages. The hosts interpret it as a symbolic retelling of the founding of Babylon, where humanity's attempt to unite and build a tower to heaven is thwarted by God, who confuses their language and scatters them.

concepts.title: Babylon as the Archetypal Empire
concepts.summary: Babylon is presented as the first world empire and the archetype of all subsequent empires, characterized by the attempt to unite humanity under a single rule, often through conquest and idolatry. The hosts trace this pattern from Babylon to Rome and modern empires, seeing it as a recurring spiritual reality.

concepts.title: Division of the Nations
concepts.summary: The division of humanity into 70 nations at the Tower of Babel is seen as an act of God, who appointed angelic beings (sons of God) to govern these nations. This concept is rooted in Deuteronomy 32:8 and is central to understanding the spiritual dynamics of the world.

concepts.title: Angelic Governance of Nations
concepts.summary: The idea that angels were assigned to govern the nations after Babel, but many fell and became demons, leading to idolatry and corruption. This concept is supported by Deuteronomy 32:8, Psalm 82, and early Christian writers like Eusebius and Dionysius the Areopagite.

concepts.title: Theosis (Deification)
concepts.summary: The ultimate destiny of humanity is to become like God, participating in His divine nature and taking up the roles of the fallen angels in governing creation. This is seen as the fulfillment of the promises to Abraham and the goal of salvation.

claims.text: The Tower of Babel story is a biblical retelling of the founding of Babylon, not a separate event. The name 'Babel' is the Hebrew form of 'Babylon'.
The biblical etymology of Babel from the Hebrew 'balal' (to confuse) is a deliberate pun, not a mistaken etymology, serving as a theological commentary on Babylon.
Babylon was founded around 2300 BC, as confirmed by archaeological evidence and ancient sources, including Berossus and Pliny.
Babylon under Hammurabi was the first world empire, uniting Mesopotamia and creating a vast trade network that connected the known world.
The Tower of Babel represents humanity's attempt to bring God down to serve their own purposes, and God's response was to scatter them and appoint angels over the nations.
After Babel, God divided humanity into 70 nations and assigned them to angelic beings (sons of God), as stated in Deuteronomy 32:8.
Many of the angels assigned to the nations fell and became demons, leading the nations into idolatry and corruption, as described in Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 82.
Christ came to defeat the demonic powers that had enslaved the nations, fulfilling the promise of Deuteronomy 32:43 and liberating humanity from their influence.
All land promises to Abraham's descendants were fulfilled in the conquest of Canaan, as stated in Joshua 21:43-45, and there are no outstanding land promises to any ethnic nation.
The ultimate destiny of the saints is to replace the fallen angels in governing creation, as seen in Revelation 20:4 and the promise of thrones in Matthew 19:28.
